newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mercedes-Benz says can overcome disruptions.
newsitem.headline: Mercedes-Benz says can overcome disruptions.

text.p: Mercedes-Benz AG chief executive Helmut Werner said on Monday that the German luxury carmaker can make up without difficulty production lost so far due to strikes over changes in sick-pay benefits.
In an interview with Reuters at the Paris car show, Werner said protest strikes had disrupted the production of 2,500 vehicles but that Mercedes would be able to overcome the lost production.
"I am of the opinion that we can make this up," Werner said, noting that vehicle sales so far had been going according to plan.
Mercedes workers at three major factories stayed away from work on Saturday in protest at the company's decision to cut sick pay from October 1, the engineering union IG Metall said.

Only a few hundred of a total staff of 20,000 at the plants in Sindelfingen, Untertuerkheim and Bremen turned up for work after the works council suspended an agreement to work extra Saturday shifts to cope with high demand.
The union plans another day of protests next Tuesday.

Mercedes's parent, Daimler-Benz AG, was the first German industrial group to announce it would enforce a 20 percent cut in sick pay from October 1 for its 220,000 workers. Several big companies, including Siemens AG, have followed suit.
Werner said he was optimistic that a resolution of the labour strife would be reached, adding that any pact would be beneficial to both sides.
"I am convinced that we will come to a good solution," Werner said.

Werner declined to say how much Mercedes could save by the reduced payouts for sick pay, saying German workers already enjoyed generous holiday allowances and other benefits that made Germany a difficult place in which to operate.
In addition, Werner said the group's financial performance so far during 1996 had been positively influenced by the recent appreciation of the dollar.
"This year compared to the last few years we have had a positive influence," Werner said of the mark's depreciation.
Werner repeated his expectation that the car and truck maker would report 1996 sales of about 75 billion marks ($49 billion).
He said that Mercedes would continue to focus on foreign markets but that it would not endanger German jobs.
